cells.tense: You are keeping something steady that came out of a change, and you know how to keep it.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you did not do alone, and let their yes sit without taking it back.
cells.core:
You made something real out of a messy stretch, and now you're keeping it steady. Not frozen — held. You know which part is worth keeping and how to keep it from getting knocked over. That's a skill and you're using it.

The tricky part is that when something settles, it can feel finished. But the keeping still has a next move. You read how the pieces fit better than most people in the room. That reading works better when someone else can see it too. Say the shape out loud once, not to check it, just to let it land. You'll find out what holds when another person can see it with you.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to keep what you made. Let someone else see its shape.
cells.verb: holding what a change produced before it can be shared
cells.place: a place where you see the shape of things without any of their weight

cells.tense: You will have mapped every way this slips before it has had a chance to slip at all.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're keeping and leave it untouched for a day. Do not adjust it.
cells.core:
You're guarding something so far ahead of time that the guarding has become the work. Every possible drift, every small slip, gets mapped and pre-solved. The shape you're protecting is real, but the attention is running on a future that hasn't happened, and the thing itself is getting less of you than the worry is.

When you pull back, you're left with what's actually here: something made, something solid, something that can take a little air. It doesn't need you hovering to stay whole. Let one piece sit unmanaged. If it shifts, that's information, not loss. What you're keeping is tougher than the bracing shows you.

cells.tense: You stopped picking things up a while back, and you are still standing at that spot.
cells.ask: Take one thing that's already yours and put it where you can see it. Leave it there.
cells.core:
There's something you made or came through, and you've stopped handling it. The ending before it took a lot, and holding anything after that felt like it would take more. So the pattern is still clear — you can see how things fit — but your hands aren't on it. You're watching a shape you know well and not touching it.

What brings you back isn't a big push. It's one small, concrete move: a thing you can point to, done by you, that you don't immediately hand off or explain away. Start with what already exists. You don't need a new shape yet. You need your grip back on the old one.

cells.tense: You are the one keeping this steady, and you talk about it as if steadiness were just the weather.
cells.ask: Say 'I kept this' once about something that is still upright because you held it.
cells.core:
You've been keeping the shape of this for a while, and you've stopped counting it as yours. In conversations it comes out as just how things are, or the way the team works, or luck. But someone made the decisions that kept it together, and that someone is you. You just don't claim it.

You may hear that as plain fact-telling rather than avoidance. Either way, the work is real, the pattern is real, and it runs on your attention. The one thing you haven't done is mark it. Not in a big announcement — just in your own head. One sentence, said plainly, that puts your name on what you carried.

attempts.check: The kernel calls this the peaceful holding of something real, but the only support is the status and the card — no evidence that a transformation has actually produced something in this person's life. The ask still works even if the read is wrong: it's just 'hand the map to one person' — if the balance isn't perfect, they still get feedback or a concrete moment, and the offer doesn't depend on the diagnosis. The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'map in the drawer' line in Balanced — it flatters the reader-as-seer while making the person's own holding feel like an artifact, so I fixed it to keep the person's ownership intact.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that a transformation has actually produced something worth preserving in this person's life — the record gives the card and the status but no biography. A reader could reasonably say nothing was won, nothing needs holding. The asks survive being wrong: each is one visible move that returns something to the person's own hands whether or not my read fits. The sentence serving the writer more than the person was the 'map you've been reading' line, which flattered the reader as seer; it is gone.
